documents: Underwood, Dugan & Cardona (2022), How clay mineral assemblages affect instability on the upper slope of the Hikurangi subduction zone, New Zealand, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL100529 (published PDF, 13 pp.)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 13), which match PDF pages counted from 1

entry.evidence: Given that long list, the challenge with any individual occurrence is to isolate and quantify the impact of each variable.

sequences.source_document: Underwood et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: Pose the question of whether clay composition has a demonstrable influence on the frictional properties of trench-slope sediments prone to landsliding.
steps.quote: The relevance to studies of landslides on the trench slope is to test whether clays have any demonstrable influence on frictional properties.

steps.action: Report the published rival for Tuaheni creep: gas-hydrate occlusion of permeability causing overpressure and hydrofracturing, or plastic deformation of hydrate-bearing sediment.
steps.quote: one hypothesis is that occlusion of permeability by gas hydrate

steps.action: Set aside gas-hydrate dynamics as the main destabilizer, using shipboard hydrate detection only below 100 mbsf and published numerical modeling.
steps.quote: gas-hydrate dynamics are unlikely as the main destabilizing variable

steps.action: Frame the rival to be tested: compositional excursions at the inferred slip surfaces and weak layers reduced friction and shear strength preferentially along those layers.
steps.quote: testing whether excursions in composition are large enough to have reduced the sediment's frictional properties and shear strength preferentially along any layers

steps.action: Apply the authors' previously published XRD protocol: glycol-saturated oriented clay aggregates (<2 μm), regression equations from standard mixtures, and published absolute errors.
steps.quote: values of normalized relative mineral abundance were computed using a set of regression equations that relate wt% values to peak area

steps.action: Design the sampling (mud only, coarser interbeds avoided, samples abutting geotechnical whole rounds) and fix the significance threshold at the method's absolute errors.
steps.quote: Compositional differences among individual specimens, or between lithologic units, are not regarded as geologically significant unless they exceed those errors.

steps.action: Measure clay assemblages in 76 specimens from Site U1519 and report unit statistics, with smectite dominant (average 53 wt%) and little scatter.
steps.quote: [...] from Site U1519 reveal unusually small amounts of compositional scatter

steps.action: Measure 99 specimens from Site U1517 (Tuaheni landslide) and report unit-by-unit statistics, with smectite dominant (average 52 wt%).
steps.quote: Smectite is the most abundant clay mineral (site average = 52 wt%)

steps.action: Compare clay-fraction composition at the horizons of interest (~31, ~41, ~66 mbsf) against the error threshold and find the shifts within error.
steps.quote: are trivial, however, and within the method's normal error range

steps.action: Convert the normalized clay abundances to bulk-sediment mineral concentrations using shipboard total-clay data (bulk smectite average 21 wt%), judged more diagnostic for friction.
steps.quote: We regard concentrations of individual minerals in bulk sediment to be more [...]

steps.action: Compare bulk concentrations across unit boundaries and suspected slip surfaces and find no excursions beyond background scatter.
steps.quote: excursions are absent at the suspected slip surfaces

steps.action: Use coeval unit I strata at Site U1519 as a reference site unaffected by landslides and find them compositionally similar.
steps.quote: Coeval strata at Site U1519 (unit I) are similar

steps.action: Analyze 30 specimens from piston and gravity cores along the slope to extend spatial coverage, and find more smectite in the NE than in the SW.
steps.quote: Samples from the NE corner of the study area generally contain more smectite (and less illite) compared to those to the SW

steps.action: Reconstruct provenance from published geology and river sediment yields (TVZ and East Cape smectite sources, illitic basement and Waipaoa sources) and explain the assemblage by current blending.
steps.quote: appears to be a product of blending among suspensions emanating from multiple sources, with transport by the WCC and ECC.

steps.action: Estimate residual angles of internal friction from bulk smectite with the Tiwari & Marui (2005) empirical curves, first binary and then the preferred ternary curve (about 5.9° average, 3.8° minimum).
steps.quote: our calculated values for bulk %-smectite translate to predictions of 5.9° (average) and 3.8° for the minimum angle of internal friction

steps.action: List published weak-layer mechanisms from elsewhere (tephra beds, smectitic alteration of glass, pore-pressure focusing, fabric realignment, hydrogeologic contrasts, anomalous porosity at the Tuaheni base).
steps.quote: In some examples, tephra beds act as weak layers

steps.action: Reject a compositional cause (ash bed, high total clay, high smectite) for the slip surfaces at ~41 and ~59 mbsf and for the weak layer at ~31 mbsf.
steps.quote: Surprisingly, we found no evidence at Site U1517 for pronounced compositional variations within or across any of the weak layers or inferred slip surfaces.

steps.action: Adopt published explanations for the remaining features: a climate- and current-driven facies change at the unit III/IV boundary, and formation of the ~31 mbsf weak layer by fabric realignment during slip.
steps.quote: That weak layer probably developed during a slip event via realignment of phyllosilicate grain fabric (Crutchley et al., 2022).

steps.action: Keep the claim that uniform smectite-rich composition preconditions the whole Tuaheni succession to fail, with flatter gradients explaining the stability at U1519, while noting that direct friction tests are warranted.
steps.quote: seems to have preconditioned the Tuaheni strata to fail without layer-specific weaknesses

steps.action: Compare the along-strike decrease of smectite in the ECC direction with the published density of landslide scars (Watson et al., 2020).
steps.quote: The frequency of landslide scars decreases where proportions of illite and chlorite are higher

steps.action: Conclude that smectite abundance and slide-scar density both decrease downstream of the ECC, so dispersal systems can impart strike-parallel changes in slope instability.
steps.quote: Smectite abundance and slide scars both decrease toward the SW

tree.answer: Abundant submarine landslides on the Hikurangi margin; Tuaheni slip surfaces and weak layers of debated origin
Clay composition measured directly by XRD; friction not measured, inferred from an empirical relation
Test whether clay composition weakens sediment preferentially along slip layers
Layer-specific compositional weakness vs uniform preconditioning; gas hydrate, pore pressure and fabric realignment named
Yes: compositional excursions at slip surfaces vs none beyond XRD error
Conditions found: existing IODP drill cores and piston cores

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Along-strike piston cores and landslide-scar density give a qualitative spatial co-variation
Partly: reference site U1519 and two friction curves; no direct friction tests
Compositional excursion rival rejected; uniform compositional preconditioning kept

end.claim: Smectite-rich, compositionally homogeneous mud weakens the whole Tuaheni succession (friction angle about 6° on average) with no compositional excursions at slip surfaces or weak layers, so factors other than composition decide where slip nucleates.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the densely sampled XRD record of 99 specimens across the Tuaheni slip surfaces at Site U1517, the absence of compositional excursions, and with it the claim of uniform preconditioning, could not be stated.

gates.evidence: Action: continuous coring at U1517 was designed to cross the interpreted slide décollement, debris base and gas-hydrate base 'To test those ideas' (others' gas-hydrate hypotheses, p. 3), but the clay samples merely abut whole rounds taken for other tests (p. 5). Claim: the no-excursion result could have failed, because excursions at ~31, ~41, ~59 and ~66 mbsf were looked for (pp. 5, 8). Registration: the significance threshold was fixed beforehand from the published XRD errors (p. 5), and the horizons of interest were defined beforehand from seismic and shipboard data; no analysis plan is stated.

imports.item: Tiwari & Marui (2005) empirical relation between smectite content and residual angle of internal friction

limits: Friction is never measured: the angles of 5.9° and 3.8° come from an external empirical curve, and the authors concede 'direct tests of frictional properties are warranted' (p. 8). Status of the friction values: estimate_with_resolution, but without propagated uncertainty. The along-strike link between smectite and landslide scars rests on 30 piston-core specimens and published scar maps with no statistical test; status regularity_in_range, qualitative. The provenance-blending account is best_explanation from literature synthesis. The weak-layer origin (fabric realignment) is adopted from Crutchley et al. (2022), not tested here. U1519 recovery was poor (~55%) with large gaps. Mud-only sampling avoided coarse interbeds, so thin compositional anomalies in ash or sand beds would be missed; whether this matters is not discussed. No review history was supplied. Coding the action gate 'partly' is an inference from the drilling rationale.

disagreements.target: Crutchley et al. (2022): the basal shear zone exploited a pre-existing weak layer
disagreements.support: The XRD data show no compositional anomaly at the slip surfaces or the weak layer, and the paper attributes the ~31 mbsf weak layer to fabric realignment during slip rather than inherited stratigraphy.
disagreements.quote: Crutchley et al. (2022) contended that the basal shear zone of the Tuaheni slide exploited a pre-existing weak layer

disagreements.target: Gas-hydrate destabilization hypothesis for the Tuaheni landslide (Mountjoy, Pecher, et al., 2014; Crutchley et al., 2010; Ellis et al., 2010)
disagreements.support: Cited evidence only: hydrate was detected below 100 mbsf, and Screaton et al. (2019) modeling, not new data from this paper.
disagreements.quote: gas-hydrate dynamics are unlikely as the main destabilizing variable

disagreements.target: Tephra and altered volcanic layers as weak layers and glide planes (Harders et al., 2010; Miramontes et al., 2018; Kuhlmann [...]
disagreements.support: At Tuaheni none of the slip or weak intervals coincides with an ash bed or high smectite, so the mechanism does not apply here.
disagreements.quote: None of those intervals coincides with a bed of volcanic ash, or unusually high amounts of total clay, or unusually high concentrations of smectite

alternatives_considered.chosen: Three-component quartz-smectite-kaolinite curve of Tiwari & Marui (2005)
alternatives_considered.reason: provides a more realistic match for Hikurangi bulk sediment

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normalized relative abundances in the clay-sized fraction

alternatives_considered.chosen: Margin-parallel currents (WCC, ECC) blending suspensions from multiple sources
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Sediment gravity flows (unconfined turbidity currents, canyon funneling)
alternatives_considered.reason: compositional homogeneity and the along-strike smectite trend fit routing by currents
